title: Exported receiver executes arbitrary shell commands from an unauthenticated broadcast
evidence: AndroidManifest.xml receiver com.keenon.systemservice.SysServiceBroadcastReceiver, no android:exported but has <intent-filter> and targetSdkVersion=22 -> exported by default; no android:permission on the receiver. JADX decompile of SysServiceBroadcastReceiver.onReceive: `if (ServiceDefine.ServiceIntent.ACTION_EXE_CMD.equals(str)) { exeCmd(intent.getStringExtra(KEY_KEENON_DATA)); }`; exeCmd() runs on a pool thread via Lcom/keenon/peanut/core/utils/device/ShellUtil;->exeCmdSync(String) (disassembly: ProcessBuilder{"sh"} / writes the extra text then "exit\n"), result broadcast via com.keenon.action.EXECUTE_CMD_RESULT.
impact: Any app on the device (no permission required) can send this broadcast and have ServiceSystem execute an arbitrary shell command string as the app's process UID, which per sharedUserId=android.uid.system is intended to run as system. This is an arbitrary command execution primitive with no caller authentication.
remediation: Require a signature-level custom permission on the receiver, verify the sending package/UID (getCallingUid via a bound service instead of a broadcast), and remove free-form shell execution from the IPC surface in favor of a fixed set of validated operations.
description: SysServiceBroadcastReceiver is exported by default (targetSdk<31 + intent-filter) and dispatches android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED, com.keenon.action.IMPORT_U_DRIVE_DATA, .SILENT_INSTALL_APP and .EXECUTE_CMD with no permission check. The EXECUTE_CMD branch takes the KEY_KEENON_DATA extra and hands it to a shell.
reproduction: Static: send `am broadcast -a com.keenon.action.EXECUTE_CMD --es keenon_data '<cmd>'` from any installed app (not executed here; reproduction is inferred from code, not observed).

title: Exported receiver copies arbitrary files/directories on request
evidence: JADX: `if (ServiceDefine.ServiceIntent.ACTION_IMPORT_U_DRIVER_FILE.equals(str)) { copyFile(intent.getStringExtra(KEY_FORM_PATH), intent.getStringExtra(KEY_TO_PATH)); }`; copyFile logs 'start copyFile %s to %s' and calls Lcom/keenon/peanut/core/utils/io/FileUtil;->copyFile/copyDirFiles with attacker-supplied source/destination strings (disassembly of FileUtil.copyFile(File,File,int) and copyDirFiles).
impact: Any app can trigger a file/directory copy between two paths of its choosing, limited only by the system-UID process's filesystem permissions; no path validation observed.
remediation: Restrict to a fixed allow-listed source directory (e.g. only the actual U-disk mount) and a fixed destination, verify caller identity, and canonicalize/validate paths against path traversal.
description: Companion branch to SYS-001 in the same unauthenticated receiver.
reproduction: Static: send the IMPORT_U_DRIVE_DATA broadcast with formPath/toPath extras (not executed).

title: Exported receiver triggers the package-install flow for a caller-supplied path
component: ServiceSystem: SysServiceBroadcastReceiver (action com.keenon.action.SILENT_INSTALL_APP) + peanut core AppInstallerUtil
evidence: JADX onReceive: ACTION_SILENT_INSTALL_APP branch reads KEY_FORM_PATH, checks File(path).exists(), then calls Lcom/keenon/peanut/core/utils/android/AppInstallerUtil;->installApp(Context,String) which builds an ACTION_VIEW intent with FileProvider / vnd.android.package-archive and startActivity (disassembly). A separate installAppSilenceVLL overload (`pm install -r `) exists in the same class but is not the one invoked from this receiver (STRONGLY_SUPPORTED, invoke-list shows installApp not installAppSilence called here).
impact: Any app can cause the system to open the package installer UI for an arbitrary local file path; actual install still needs user confirmation via the installer UI (INFERRED, since the invoked overload is the ACTION_VIEW one, not the shell pm install one, for this code path).
remediation: Require a signature permission on the receiver; if silent install is intended, gate installAppSilence behind the same control as SYS-001/002.
description: Third unauthenticated action on the exported receiver.

title: Unauthenticated exported AIDL services allow arbitrary MQTT publish/subscribe and voice/TTS control
evidence: AndroidManifest.xml: all four services declared android:exported="true" with no android:permission. Bundled .aidl interface files (com/keenon/{voice,tts,aidl/mqtt,bi/aidl}) define execCmd/execCmdAsync, startTts, publish/subscribe/observer with caller-chosen String topic and String appFlag, and IBiManager.send(event, properties, ap, versionName). MqttAidlApiImpl.publish/subscribe forward directly to Lcom/keenon/component/core/mqtt/MqttApiProxy;->publish/subscribe without a topic allow-list (dexscan invoke list for MqttAidlApiImpl).
impact: Any app that knows the AIDL interfaces (shipped inside the APK, trivially extractable) can bind these services without any permission and publish to, or receive from, arbitrary MQTT topics under the device's cloud identity, inject BI events, and drive TTS/voice behavior.
remediation: Add a signature-level permission to each <service>, validate caller UID/package against an allow-list (peanut-clean, robot-installation-assistant, launcher), and restrict the MQTT topic namespace reachable from AIDL callers.
description: The four system services that back the vendor serviceSdk client libraries are reachable by any app on the device.
reproduction: Static only; AIDL stubs are present in both ServiceSystem and in peanut-clean/robot-installation-assistant (classes.json cls listing).

title: MQTT-delivered remote shell command execution
evidence: Disassembly of SshMqttProxy$2.onMessageArrived: payload on SshConstants.getCmdTopic() ("/android/remote/cmd/frp_%s") is turned into a String and passed to APPCmdHelper.ins().inputCmd(json). Disassembly/JADX of APPCmdHelper.inputCmd: `JSONObject(str).getString("msg")` then `ShellUtil.exeCmd(msg, callback)`; the callback (APPCmdHelper$1) logs and calls onResponseData, which publishes {isSuccess,data} back on the cmd_resp topic via SshMqttProxy.publish.
impact: Whoever can publish to the per-serial-number MQTT command topic (the vendor cloud broker, or anyone who can reach/spoof it) can execute an arbitrary shell command on the tablet as the RemoteControl process (sharedUserId android.uid.system).
remediation: Authenticate and authorize the MQTT connection end-to-end (mutual TLS/ACLs restricting publish to the device's own topic), sign/validate command payloads, and avoid free-form shell execution.
description: This is a legitimate maintenance feature by design (remote shell for support), but its security rests entirely on the MQTT broker's access control, which is outside this APK and was not analyzed.
reproduction: Static only; requires MQTT broker access, not available/attempted in this environment.

title: adb over TCP enabled unconditionally at init and reachable through the FRP tunnel
evidence: JADX decompile of SystemInitializer.init: `ShellUtil.exeCmd("setprop service.adb.tcp.port 5678\nstop adbd\nstart adbd", null);` runs unconditionally (not gated by build flavor) after the fusion-board branch. FrpClientHelper.buildFrpClientConfig/buildMapFrpClientConfig strings include `local_port = 5678` (DEX string table, FrpClientHelper ms output).
impact: adbd is switched to listen on TCP port 5678 at every ServiceSystem init, and the vendor FRP tunnel forwards that same local port to a remote server when triggered by MQTT (SYS-005's channel). If adb is unauthenticated (ro.adb.secure=0) or the key is pre-authorized, this exposes a full adb shell to whoever controls the FRP/cloud path.
remediation: Do not expose adb over TCP in production; if needed for support, gate it behind a short-lived, explicitly user-approved flow, and never bridge it through an externally reachable tunnel.
description: The same constant (5678) appears both as the adb TCP port set at boot and as the frpc local_port, which combined with the exported FRP flow is a built-in remote-adb layer.
reproduction: Static correlation of two constants; not dynamically verified.

title: Hard-coded SMB root credentials for the robot-side host
evidence: Disassembly of SMBManager.lambda$init$0$SMBManager: `new AuthenticationContext("root", SMBInterface.PASS_LIST[passIndex].toCharArray(), "DOMAIN")` then `SMBClient().connect("192.168.64.20")`.authenticate(...). SMBInterface.<clinit> builds a 2-entry String[] PASS_LIST with filled-new-array of two short string constants (values not reproduced here; type=hard-coded password, length redacted).
impact: A fixed, reverse-engineerable root password set for the SMB server at 192.168.64.20 (the ROS/robot side host) is embedded in the APK; anyone who extracts the APK gets root SMB credentials to the robot compute unit.
remediation: Do not hard-code root credentials; use per-device provisioned, rotated credentials or certificate-based auth; least-privilege SMB account instead of root.
description: Static string/byte-code constant; exact values intentionally not printed (REDACT: 2 string constants, class com.keenon.peanut.uploadlog.smb.SMBInterface, field PASS_LIST).

title: Hard-coded third-party LLM API bearer keys in code
evidence: dexscan string extraction, KimiChatApi#initUrlConnectionAuthVL: Authorization header literal "Bearer sk-<REDACTED 51 chars>" alongside getLLMChatApiUrl()=https://api.moonshot.cn/v1/chat/completions; DeepseekChatApi#initUrlConnectionAuthVL: "Bearer sk-<REDACTED 32 hex chars>" alongside getLLMChatApiUrl()=https://dashscope.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1/chat/completions (model string "deepseek-v3").
impact: API keys for Moonshot (Kimi) and Alibaba DashScope (DeepSeek proxy) are embedded in plaintext in the DEX and usable by anyone who extracts the APK, enabling quota abuse/cost exposure, and potential impersonation of the vendor's NLP account.
remediation: Move LLM keys server-side; the app should call a Keenon-operated proxy that holds the real provider keys, not embed them.
description: REDACT: type=API key (Bearer token), location=Lcom/keenon/systemservice/voice/ctrl/nlp/kimi/KimiChatApi;->initUrlConnectionAuthVL and .../deepseek/DeepseekChatApi;->initUrlConnectionAuthVL. Values not reproduced.

title: Hard-coded Azure OpenAI / Speech keys for 8 regions in a bundled asset
evidence: JSON asset contains 8 entries (Japan East Free, Japan East, US East, Europe West, Australia East, Brazil South, South Africa North, UAE North), each with openaiKey, speechKey (both 84-character base64-like secrets) plus openaiDomain/speechDomain host names (*.openai.azure.com, *.api.cognitive.microsoft.com).
impact: Eight Azure OpenAI and Azure Cognitive Speech subscription keys are shipped in plaintext inside the APK assets, directly usable by anyone who extracts the file; significant abuse/cost risk and possible resource exhaustion against the vendor's Azure subscriptions.
remediation: Do not ship cloud provider keys in the client; proxy requests through a Keenon-controlled backend that holds the keys server-side and authenticates the device.
description: REDACT: type=cloud API keys (8x openaiKey, 8x speechKey), location=assets/voiceConfig/micro_resource.json inside the ServiceSystem APK. Values not reproduced.
reproduction: Static only; file is plain JSON, directly readable after unzip.

title: iFlytek robot-platform credentials and an RSA private key shipped in assets
evidence: robot.json / robot_test.json contain appId and secret fields for the iFlytek robot gateway (service.iflybot.com.cn, ws://robot.iflybot.com.cn/robot/engine/v2_2); assets/vtn/privateKey.pem is a PEM block beginning '-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----' (1700 bytes) alongside a matching publicKey.pem, referenced from assets/vtn/vtn.ini.
impact: A vendor-issued appId/secret pair and a private RSA key are embedded in the package; if used for authenticating to the iFlytek service or local VTN voice engine, their disclosure could allow quota abuse or impersonation.
remediation: Rotate these credentials if they are production-shipping secrets; avoid storing private keys in app assets; use per-device provisioning instead.
description: REDACT: type=appId/secret pair (robot.json, robot_test.json) and RSA private key (assets/vtn/privateKey.pem). Values not reproduced.

title: Process-wide trust-all TLS and hostname verifier
evidence: Disassembly: AllowX509TrustManager.checkClientTrusted/checkServerTrusted bodies are `return-void` (no checks); AllowX509TrustManager$1.verify(String,SSLSession) returns `const/4 v1,#1; return v1` (always true); allowAllSSL() calls HttpsURLConnection.setDefaultHostnameVerifier(this) and setDefaultSSLSocketFactory(ctx.getSocketFactory()), i.e. it replaces the JVM-wide defaults.
impact: Once SecurityKeyManager.init runs, every HttpsURLConnection in the process (not just the intended call) accepts any TLS certificate for any hostname, enabling trivial man-in-the-middle interception/tampering of HTTPS traffic from this app.
remediation: Never install a trust-all manager/hostname verifier; use proper certificate pinning or the platform default trust store for the control-plane traffic that needs it.
description: Global, not scoped to one connection.

title: MQTT TLS trust check is a substring match on certificate subject, not real validation
evidence: Disassembly of DynamicMqttServer$2.checkTrusted(X509Certificate[]): for each cert, `getSubjectDN().toString()` is checked with `String.contains("keenon.com")`; if any certificate in the chain lacks that substring, a CertificateException is thrown, otherwise the chain is accepted - there is no chain-of-trust, expiry or hostname validation. ClientSSLSocketFactory$1 (RemoteControl) performs the identical pattern for its MQTT TLS connection.
impact: An attacker who can present any certificate whose Subject DN happens to contain the literal string "keenon.com" (e.g. a self-signed cert with CN=notkeenon.com.attacker.example or any field containing that substring) will be trusted by the MQTT TLS layer, defeating certificate validation for the MQTT broker connection used for remote commands, telemetry and log notification topics.
remediation: Use standard X509 chain validation against a pinned CA, and match the full expected hostname/CN exactly rather than a substring.
description: Both apps implement the same flawed pattern, likely shared code lineage.

title: Cleartext transports and cleartext permitted at the application level
component: ServiceSystem and RemoteControl manifests (android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"); multiple http:// and tcp:// (non-TLS MQTT) endpoints
evidence: AndroidManifest.xml <application usesCleartextTraffic="true"> on both ServiceSystem and RemoteControl. String evidence: http://console.peanut.keenonrobot.com:80, http://corrector.keenonrobot.com:80, http://robotnlp.keenonrobot.com:80, http://iss.openspeech.cn/v, tcp://console.peanut.keenonrobot.com (SshMqttServer, RemotePeanutServer default URLs), Sentry DSN meta-data uses http:// scheme.
impact: Several control-plane and telemetry channels run over plaintext HTTP/TCP, exposing data (and in the MQTT/EXECUTE_CMD cases, command traffic) to network-level interception or tampering when the device is on an untrusted network.
remediation: Move all traffic to TLS with certificate pinning; remove usesCleartextTraffic=true and add a proper network_security_config enforced from the manifest (the existing one in ServiceSystem is not referenced - see SYS-014-adjacent gap note).
description: Cross-cutting network hygiene finding.

title: Generic/shared platform signing identity across system-privileged apps
evidence: certinfo.py: all three APKs (plus peanut-clean) share one v1 certificate, subject/issuer 'C=US, ST=California, L=Mountain View, O=Android, OU=Android, CN=Android, E=android@android.com', serial 00ff0641323cf95512, SHA-256 2d370c21f5dfd553d2a796314b70925fb38adeef90864c920bbbbb12887d3522, validity 2014-12-23..2042-05-10. robot-installation-assistant uses a different cert (CN=keenon).
impact: Because sharedUserId=android.uid.system requires a matching platform signature, any party possessing this well-known-pattern 'Android' test/AOSP-style key (common on many AOSP-derived platform builds) could in principle sign and install a package sharing the same UID and permissions as these apps on a device using this same platform key. Whether this specific private key is restricted to the vendor's build pipeline is UNKNOWN (could not be assessed statically); using a generic AOSP-style subject name for a platform key is itself a code-smell suggesting it may originate from a shared/public Rockchip SDK signing key rather than a vendor-unique one.
remediation: Confirm the platform signing key is unique and tightly controlled by the OEM/vendor build process; if it is a widely distributed Rockchip SDK test key, replace it with a vendor-unique platform key.
description: Evidence is limited to certificate metadata; private key custody could not be assessed.

title: krlog's sharedUserId is declared on <application>, not <manifest>
evidence: Decoded manifest: `<application android:... android:sharedUserId="android.uid.system" ...>` - the attribute appears on the <application> element; the <manifest> root element has no sharedUserId attribute in the same decode.
impact: The Android platform parses sharedUserId only from <manifest>; if this is indeed how the binary XML is structured (not a decoder artifact), krlog would install with its own UID, not the shared system UID, meaning its READ_LOGS/INSTALL_PACKAGES/DELETE_PACKAGES/READ_PRIVILEGED_PHONE_STATE permission requests would only succeed if independently granted as privileged/signature permissions by the platform. This could be either a packaging defect (unintentionally weaker app) or the decoder's attribute-sorting may simply place it under the nearest preceding start-tag in this minimal parser - verification against the installed device's process UID is needed.
remediation: Verify sharedUserId placement with a canonical AAPT/apktool decode and, on a test device, check the running UID of com.keenon.krlog; correct the manifest if the placement is wrong.
description: Flagged as a possible manifest authoring defect; confidence is MEDIUM because it rests on one custom AXML decoder's output.
reproduction: Re-decode AndroidManifest.xml with a second independent tool (apktool/aapt2) to confirm; not done in this engagement (no apktool permitted).

title: androidx.test instrumentation activities exported in a release build
evidence: AndroidManifest.xml: all three declared with android:exported="true" and an action.MAIN intent-filter, inside the production RemoteControl manifest (not a separate androidTest APK).
impact: Test-support activities intended for instrumentation test harnesses are present and launchable in the shipped release APK; while individually low-capability, this increases attack surface and indicates androidx.test dependencies were not stripped from the release build.
remediation: Exclude androidx.test from the release build variant / use testImplementation scope only, or explicitly set exported=false for these activities in the release manifest.
description: Matches the scope item about androidx.test InstrumentationActivityInvoker exported activities in release builds.

title: Hard-coded AES/keystore material and a native key map, secrets cached in unencrypted MMKV/SharedPreferences
component: ServiceSystem/RemoteControl: lib*/libcipher_pack.so (CipherUtil.get); RemoteControl: com.keenon.common.mqtt.ClientSSLSocketFactory.create (eng flavor), com.keenon.peanut.core.security.AesUtil.generateKeyOrIV, com.keenon.common.http.manager.ConfigManager (defaultMMKV getters for mqtt user/password, security AES key/IV, RSA keys)
evidence: soinv.py: libcipher_pack.so exports data symbols BUGLY_APPID_ENG/PROD, BUGLY_APPKEY_ENG/PROD, UMENG_APPKEY and contains short plaintext string constants alongside keys such as aes_dev_key, aes_dev_iv, ssl_key_pwd_test/prod, ssl_trust_pwd_test/prod, md5_secret_key, amap_appkey, peanut_mqtt_u/p[_prod], selected via getPkgNameByContext/matchCipherStrFromMap per caller package. ClientSSLSocketFactory.create (disassembly) has two literal String constants (lengths 8 and 16; values redacted) used as keystore passwords for the eng-flavor BKS keystores. AesUtil.generateKeyOrIV uses a fixed 62-character alphabet string as its character pool (not itself a secret, but the keygen approach is visible). ConfigManager getters (getMqttUserName/Password, getSecurityAesKey/Iv, getSecurityRsaPrivate/PublicKey) read from MMKV.defaultMMKV(), which is not configured with encryption in the traced call (MMKV supports AES-encrypted stores but no encryption key argument was observed at the call sites examined).
impact: A static, extractable key/credential map keyed only by caller package name provides limited protection (obfuscation, not a secret boundary); eng-flavor MQTT TLS keystore passwords are plaintext constants; and runtime-resolved secrets (MQTT password, AES key/IV, RSA keys) are cached in an MMKV store that, as called, does not appear to use MMKV's own encryption option, making them readable by anything with root/backup access to app data.
remediation: Use Android Keystore-backed secrets instead of a static native lookup table; never ship symmetric keystore passwords in code; enable MMKV encryption (or use EncryptedSharedPreferences) for any cached secret.
description: REDACT: type=multiple hard-coded key labels/short secrets inside libcipher_pack.so and ClientSSLSocketFactory.create. Values not reproduced beyond already-public-looking labels (BUGLY/UMENG are commonly public SDK app IDs, not necessarily sensitive by themselves).
reproduction: Static only (ELF export table + string scan + disassembly).

title: allowBackup=true on all three system apps
evidence: AndroidManifest.xml <application android:allowBackup="true"> in ServiceSystem, RemoteControl and krlog; no android:fullBackupContent restriction observed.
impact: If adb backup / auto backup is reachable (requires USB debugging or an account-backed backup; mitigated if adb is secured), app data including cached secrets (MMKV/SharedPreferences, see SYS-017) and logs could be extracted.
remediation: Set allowBackup=false for privileged system components, or scope backups to exclude secret-bearing files.
description: Low severity on its own; compounds SYS-006 (adb exposure) and SYS-017 (cached secrets).

title: Secrets written to logcat, which krlog then stores persistently on shared storage
component: ServiceSystem: com.keenon.component.core.mqtt.DynamicMqttServer.getKeyPwd/getTrustPwd (debug logging); krlog: com.keenon.krlog.utils.LogcatHelper (captures `logcat` to files)
evidence: Disassembly of DynamicMqttServer.getKeyPwd(String): after resolving the password via CipherUtil.get, it calls KLogProxy$ModuleLogger.d(tag, "getKeyPwd %s => %s", [param, resolvedValue]) - the resolved password value is passed as a format argument to a debug log call. krlog's LogcatHelper$LogDumper runs `logcat` and writes every line verbatim to /sdcard/krlog/... files (section 4.3).
impact: If this debug log level is active, resolved keystore passwords are written to the system log, and krlog's full-device logcat capture would persist them in plaintext files on external storage, which can then be exported via USB (krlog UI) or uploaded by RemoteControl's log-upload feature.
remediation: Never log secret values, even at debug level; add log scrubbing for known sensitive keys before any log is persisted or uploaded.
description: Chain of two otherwise-separate apps' behavior combining into a disclosure path.
reproduction: Static only; log level gating (whether debug logs are compiled/enabled in production) not verified.

title: Remote desktop with input injection launched from a world-writable-adjacent temp path
evidence: JADX decompile: `ClientSdkManager.LaunchExternalProcess(this.mSandboxPath, LOCAL_TEMP_PATH, "liborayinput_agent5.so", " -o 0", false)` and similar, with LOCAL_TEMP_PATH referencing /data/local/tmp/ (string evidence: '/data/local/tmp/'). INJECT_EVENTS permission is requested in the manifest.
impact: Native remote-control helper binaries are copied to and executed from /data/local/tmp; if that directory or the copy step is not tightly permissioned, a local attacker (e.g. another app with shell access) could race or substitute the binary. The remote desktop feature itself grants a cloud-authenticated operator full screen view and input injection on the tablet.
remediation: Execute helper binaries from the app's private directory (filesDir) rather than /data/local/tmp, verify binary integrity (signature/hash) before exec, and ensure INJECT_EVENTS usage is gated by the same authentication as session creation.
description: Design-level: remote-control/input-injection functionality is powerful by nature; the main static concern is the use of a shared temp path.

title: Cloud-controlled nginx/map config deployment with native shell helper and no observed filename validation
evidence: JADX decompile of handleNginxFile: file/fileName and certificate.file/certificate.fileName come directly from the parsed MQTT JSON payload (FrpNginxMapConfigBean.NginxConfig) and are concatenated into shell-style commands run through KNNativeTool.nativeCmd: `/system/bin/cp <BASE_PATH><certFileName> <MAP_NGINX_PEM_DIR>/<certFileName>`, `/system/bin/unzip /oem/etc/ros/runtime/remotemap/<certFileName> -d <MAP_NGINX_PEM_DIR>/`, `/system/bin/cp <BASE_PATH><fileName> <MAP_NGINX_CONFIG_DIR>/<fileName>`, finishing with `/system/bin/ubuntu1604 xargs nginx -s reload`; libnativetool.so (ELF import list) imports socket/sendto/recvfrom and exposes one JNI export nativeCmd, consistent with a local command-proxy socket rather than a direct shell exec (dexscan/elfinfo evidence); the exact transport/validation inside the native proxy was not decompiled.
impact: Filenames taken from a cloud-delivered MQTT message are embedded into constructed command strings for cp/unzip/nginx reload; if the native proxy does not itself sanitize them, this is a path-traversal / command-injection surface reachable by whoever can publish to the FRP MQTT command channel (same trust boundary as SYS-005).
remediation: Validate/escape all filenames from untrusted payloads before use in any command string, and prefer parameterized file operations (Java File APIs) over shelling out to cp/unzip.
description: The actual sanitization, if any, happens inside the native nativeCmd proxy, which was not reverse engineered beyond its import table; severity/likelihood could not be fully confirmed.
reproduction: Static only; native proxy behavior NOT_ANALYZED.

title: Exported voice deep-link activities and boot receivers (lower-severity exported surface)
component: ServiceSystem: voice.config.VoiceConfigActivity, voice.config.VoiceActivationActivity (scheme keenon://solution.scene.voice/*); RemoteControl: daemon.RobotBootReceiver, HeadService, CommonService; krlog: AutoStartBroadcastReceiver, LogService
evidence: AndroidManifest.xml: VoiceConfigActivity/VoiceActivationActivity exported=true with VIEW/BROWSABLE intent-filters on the keenon:// scheme; RobotBootReceiver/HeadService exported by default (BOOT_COMPLETED filter / explicit exported=true); krlog LogService exported=true, AutoStartBroadcastReceiver exported by default (BOOT_COMPLETED filter).
impact: These components accept external Intents/links with limited but non-zero effect (open config UI, start/stop log capture, keep-alive). Individually low risk; included for completeness of the exported-component inventory.
remediation: Review whether each truly needs to be exported; set exported=false where only internal use is intended.
description: General exported-surface hygiene item distinct from the high-severity command/file findings above.

title: Full device logcat persisted to shared external storage with no file-level access control
evidence: Disassembly/JADX: LogcatHelper$LogDumper captures all of `logcat` (not app-scoped) into /sdcard/krlog/... text files, rotated/zipped; MainActivity exports these to a USB stick found by scanning /storage/*.
impact: Any app with READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE (broadly granted pre-scoped-storage on targetSdk 22) can read the same log files that may contain other apps' sensitive log lines (see SYS-019), and a user with physical USB access can export the full log history.
remediation: Store logs in app-private storage, or restrict to a dedicated, access-controlled partition; scrub known-sensitive content before export.
description: Consequence of krlog's design rather than a coding bug.

title: LLM system prompt can be overridden from a file on writable external storage
evidence: DEX string: "/sdcard/peanut/voice/gptSystemDesc.txt" found alongside the default system-role text class (init body constant) in the LLM nlp package (dexscan string table, voice/ctrl/nlp/llm constructor).
impact: If this path is read at runtime to override the LLM system prompt (not fully traced), any app or user with storage write access could change the robot assistant's persona/instructions, which is a low-severity but notable integrity issue for an AI assistant feature.
remediation: If the override capability is intentional for field customization, move it to protected app storage or validate/sign its contents; otherwise remove external-storage sourcing for prompt content.
description: The read path into this constant was not traced to a specific method in this engagement; included as INFERRED LOW-severity finding based on a strong string co-location signal.
